query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimized low‐temperature annealing promotes the precipitation of coherent L12 nanoprecipitates along phase boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys, which simultaneously increase strength and enhance room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase (e.g., FCC and B2) lamellar colonies with semi-coherent phase boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation under tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized low-temperature annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Anneal at a temperature and duration sufficient to precipitate fine, coherent L12 nanoprecipitates at phase boundaries without triggering coarsening or unwanted phase transformations; processing should be done under controlled atmospheres to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent L12 nanoprecipitates specifically decorating the phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates act as obstacles to crack propagation and serve as additional sites for dislocation pinning, leading to enhanced precipitation strengthening and increased dislocation storage. This helps in arresting or delaying microcrack initiation and propagation while augmenting work hardening during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the annealed alloy will exhibit higher yield and tensile strength along with improved ductility (greater elongation to failure), as crack initiation is suppressed and dislocation interactions are optimized.
generation.baseline: The conventional processed eutectic high-entropy alloy with semi-coherent phase boundaries lacking engineered, coherent L12 precipitates, which shows limited tensile ductility due to early microcrack formation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective provided the annealing parameters are tightly controlled; deviations (e.g., too high temperature or excessive duration leading to precipitate coarsening) or significant changes in alloy composition could negate the beneficial effects.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact optimal annealing temperature/duration window and the long-term thermal and mechanical stability of the L12 precipitates under cyclic or real-world loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set subjected to the optimized low-temperature annealing treatment and one set processed conventionally. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the presence, size, and coherence of L12 nanoprecipitates along phase boundaries in the treated samples. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure between the two sets.
measurements: TEM imaging and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) for precipitate characterization
Quantitative analysis of microcrack density and dislocation storage via post-deformation microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if TEM analysis reveals that the precipitates are either incoherent, significantly coarsened, or absent at the phase boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In particular, dense dislocation walls formed along the phase boundaries within the FCC phase, indicating that the FCC and BCC phase boundaries acted as strong barriers for dislocation motion. The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading. reading.lever: Apply an optimized low-temperature annealing to promote coherent L12 nanoprecipitates specifically decorating phase boundaries.
reading.why: This treatment, combining precipitation strengthening with phase boundary engineering, has been shown to arrest crack propagation and enhance dislocation storage, offering a promising route for simultaneous strength and ductility improvement in lamellar HEAs.
